content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching, 'disciple' (Greek mathētēs, 'learner' or 'pupil') primarily denotes a committed follower of Jesus Christ — one who learns from him, obeys his teaching, imitates his life, and is bound to him in personal allegiance. Symbolically, discipleship stands for the whole Christian life: self-denial, cross-bearing, obedience to Jesus' word, love for fellow believers, and fruit-bearing. In this dominant reading, 'disciple' is functionally equivalent to 'Christian' (cf. Acts 11:26), describing not merely intellectual students but apprentices whose lives are being conformed to their Master.","primary_basis":["Matthew 28:19–20 (the Great Commission: 'make disciples of all nations... teaching them to obey')","Luke 9:23 / Mark 8:34 (deny yourself, take up your cross daily, and follow me)","Luke 14:26–33 (counting the cost; whoever does not renounce all cannot be my disciple)","John 8:31–32 ('If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples')","John 13:34–35 (love for one another as the mark by which all will know you are my disciples)","John 15:8 (bearing much fruit proves you are my disciples)","Matthew 10:24–25 (a disciple is not above his teacher; it is enough to be like his teacher)","Acts 11:26 ('the disciples were first called Christians in Antioch')"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"A narrower, technical/historical sense: 'the disciples' as the Twelve specifically, the inner circle Jesus chose and commissioned as apostles. In this usage the term marks a distinct historical group rather than a symbol for all believers.","basis":["Matthew 10:1–4","Mark 3:13–19","Luke 6:13 (he chose twelve, whom he named apostles)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"A broad sociological/adherent sense: 'disciple' as any adherent of a teacher or movement in the ancient world, not uniquely Christian — e.g., disciples of John the Baptist, of the Pharisees, or of Moses; some 'disciples' of Jesus later fall away, showing the term can denote loose or provisional attachment.","basis":["Mark 2:18 (disciples of John and of the Pharisees)","John 9:28 (disciples of Moses)","John 6:60–66 (many disciples turned back and no longer walked with him)","Matthew 22:16 (Pharisees' disciples)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"A two-tier reading distinguishing 'believer' from 'disciple': in some Free Grace / dispensational teaching, discipleship is a costly, optional deeper commitment beyond saving faith, so not every Christian is a disciple. This is contested by Lordship-salvation and most mainstream interpreters, who equate disciple with genuine believer.","basis":["Luke 14:26–33 (cost-of-discipleship conditions read as beyond simple faith)","John 8:31 ('truly my disciples' read as a subset of believers)","Contrast appeals to Acts 11:26 and Matthew 28:19 by the majority view"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"A formational/imitative emphasis: disciple as 'apprentice' in spiritual formation, stressing lifelong transformation into Christlikeness (prominent in modern discipleship and spiritual-formation literature, e.g., Bonhoeffer's costly discipleship, Dallas Willard's apprenticeship language). This is an emphasis within, rather than a departure from, the dominant reading.","basis":["Luke 6:40 (everyone when fully trained will be like his teacher)","Matthew 11:29 (take my yoke and learn from me)","Romans 8:29 / 2 Corinthians 3:18 (conformity to Christ's image, used in formation literature)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Ecclesiological-representative reading in redaction criticism: the disciples in the Gospels (especially Matthew) function as literary stand-ins for the later church, so their failures, learning, and commissioning model the community's own life.","basis":["Matthew 14:28–33 and 16:5–12 (disciples' 'little faith' as paradigm for the church)","Matthew 28:16–20 (the commissioned community)"],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is broad, recognizable consensus that 'disciple' means a committed follower-learner of Jesus and, in Acts and later Christian usage, functions as a synonym for 'Christian.' The main interpretive variations concern scope (the Twelve vs. all believers vs. any adherent of any teacher) and whether discipleship is coextensive with saving faith (the Lordship/Free Grace debate). The term is more descriptive than allegorical; unlike symbols such as 'leaven' or 'water,' it has little contested figurative range — disagreements are about definition and soteriological implication rather than symbolism proper."}
